runs.text: Adu. Modo de estarem muitos à

lines.note: Tootoodo describes the manner in which many people sit or remain comfortably at ease. The first long-o mark is a circumflex and the second a caron; the Portuguese construction continues below.
Tôtǒdo iru illustrates remaining at ease. Sua vontade completes the preceding Portuguese phrase, and the new translation begins with estarem before continuing on the next row.
Completes the example as many people seated at their ease. The seated posture in assentados clarifies the Japanese iru rather than supplying a separate headword.
Tootoi is glossed as holy and wondrous. The initial is a damaged T, matching neighboring headwords, rather than OCR F; the Portuguese noun is Couſa.
This short indented row gives the contracted adverbial form belonging to tootoi above. Both the caron and final circumflex are retained as printed.

The corresponding abstract noun denotes holiness or venerableness. The first o has only an acute-like surviving stroke; the supplied circumflex is retained provisionally rather than treated as a secure acute. The detached spot near the final a may belong to the broken hook of ſ, so no extra accent is introduced.

runs.text: Tono, ou ſenhor da terra mancebo ẽ

lines.note: Tootono designates the young lord of the territory in contrast with his still-living father. The Japanese title Tono is embedded in the Portuguese explanation and remains italic as printed; the abbreviated ẽ begins the comparison continued below.

runs.text: comparação do pay que ainda eſtà viuo mas de-

lines.note: The contrast is with the father who is still alive but has relinquished government. The final de- is the first part of dexou on the next physical row, not an independent preposition.
Completes dexouja o gouerno: the father has already handed over government. The close spacing of ja is retained in the transcription rather than modernized.
Totonoi gives the intransitive forms for becoming arranged or ready. Both Portuguese reflexives describe preparation, and the abbreviated cõ- is retained without expanding the tilde.
Totonouori is equated with the preceding preparation verb. Zoosaku begins the following example and refers to construction or building work.
Zoosaku totonowotta means that the construction work was completed. The Portuguese reads Acabaranſe with the printed n; it is not silently modernized to a modern reflexive spelling.
Totonoye is the transitive verb for arranging or preparing something, contrasted with the preceding intransitive entries. The Portuguese apare- continues as aparelhar.
Meshi wo totonoyuru illustrates preparing food. The historical yuru ending is retained, and the Portuguese begins its rendering with fazer.
Completes the food-preparation example as making or preparing the meal. O comer is the nominal expression for food or eating here.

runs.text: Hum certo cordelſinho que eſtà de-

lines.note: Tottsuke is identified as a small cord used on horse equipment. The visible diminutive cordelſinho is retained, and de- continues into dependurado.

runs.text: pendurado dambas as partes das retrancas do

lines.note: The cord hangs on both sides of the breeching or rear harness. Dambas is the printed contraction, and do introduces the horse named on the next row.
Completes the harness description with the horse as possessor. This short continuation is independent physical text, not part of the next headword.
Totte denotes a handle, such as the handle of a vessel or basket. The Portuguese asa provides the concrete object-part sense.
Totte kaeshi means turning back or wheeling about. The damaged initial is T, supported by the adjacent Totte and the compound, rather than OCR long s.
The definition specifies a fleeing person turning back. The relative clause belongs with voltar or tornar a virar above.
Totte noku is first glossed as moving away or withdrawing. The inflected oita is the supplied historical principal part; retirar- continues on the next row.
After completing retirar-se, the entry adds taking something and moving off with it. The final verb is irſe, with r, rather than OCR inſe.
Totto is an adverb of degree or effective action: greatly or effectively. This concise gloss starts a new entry and does not continue the retreating verb.
Toowa concerns a spoken reply, explained by kotaye kataru. The headword begins with T, not OCR r; the Portuguese introduces the answer someone gives.
The reply may be mild or harsh. Toowa no yoi hito supplies the example of a person whose responses are good or agreeable.
The Portuguese completes the example as a man of good replies, confirming that the quality of his responses is meant.
Too-uchiwa is a round Chinese fan. The printed v in vchiua represents the initial vowel of uchiwa and is preserved.
Touo is the native numeral ten. Its spelling is kept distinct from the distance-related touo- compounds that follow.

runs.text: Lugar baixo em algum rio, ou mar

lines.note: Tooasa denotes a shallow place in a river or the sea. The following line specifies a narrow stretch that can be crossed on foot.

runs.text: estreito que ſe pode paßar a vao.

lines.note: Completes the shallow-water definition: a narrow place that can be forded. The phrase a vao explains passage through shallow water.
Toobiki names a falconry action; the example offers toobiki wo suru and the alternative tooha wo hiku. The headword has initial T, correcting OCR r.

runs.text: Voar o falcão longe, ou deſgar-

lines.note: Completes tooha wo hiku, followed by the falcon flying far away. Enlargement supports Voar and falcão, rather than OCR Voer and faltão; desgar- continues on the next row.
Completes desgarrar-se: the falcon ranges away to take a bird. This supplies the hunting purpose of the flight described above.
Toodooto is the adverb far away. The following example repeats it across the physical break, with Touo- at the end of this row.
Toodooto hikayeta describes holding oneself well back. The Portuguese says to stay at a distance, with ou- beginning ousando below.
Completes the reason for staying back: not daring to approach closely out of respect. The distance is socially deferential in this example.
Toodooshii describes something remote or distant, matching both Portuguese adjectives. The final ij is the printed adjectival ending.
Tooha wo hiku is the same falconry expression explained under Toobiki. The damaged first letter is T, not OCR F; Vide introduces the divided cross-reference To-uobiqi.
Completes the cross-reference Touobiqi from the preceding physical row. It is not a new entry or an omitted Portuguese continuation.

runs.text: Lugar, ou praya onde vaza mui-

lines.note: Toohikata describes a shore or place where the tide withdraws a long way. The Portuguese mui- continues into muito below.

runs.text: to amarè, & fica muito eſpaço em ſeco.

lines.note: Completes the tidal description: much ground is left dry. The close spelling amarè and the printed grave accent are retained rather than respaced or modernized.
Toogake is an attack made after going a considerable distance in war. The line-end mark after na is visible and retained even though the following guerra is a separate word.

runs.text: guerra indo longe adar nos inimigos. Vt,

lines.note: The attack involves travelling far to strike the enemy. The compact adar is retained; To- begins the repeated Japanese headword in the example.
Completes toogake wo suru, to conduct such an attack. The final vowel is u, producing ſuru rather than OCR ſuri.

runs.text: Couſa alongada, ou que eſtà longe.

lines.note: Tooi describes something far away or distant. The next two indented rows give related grammatical forms.

Touô is the contracted adverbial form of tooi. The example means looking into the distance, corresponding to touô miru. Its m/r strokes are badly broken, so the supplied Touôm iru and its physical gap are retained provisionally rather than silently respaced into the expected phrase; the circumflex of the head form is clear.
Toosa is the corresponding noun, distance. It is the final body line in column 1, above the bottom rule.

runs.text: O por em aperto, ou combater

lines.note: Toozeme describes putting an opponent under pressure or attacking from afar. The printed separation in Touo jeme is retained.

runs.text: de longe, como quando ſe combate a fortaleza

lines.note: Explains the distant attack through the example of fighting against a fortress. This develops the military sense of toozeme.
Completes the qualification: the attackers do not approach very closely. The negative establishes that distance is essential to this sense.

runs.text: Atalayas, ou eſpias que vão deſcobrir

lines.note: Toomi denotes lookouts or scouts who go to reconnoitre. The Portuguese verbs and nouns identify people performing reconnaissance, not simply distant eyesight.

runs.text: o campo na guerra. ¶ Itẽ, Na caça q̃ ſe faz cõ-

lines.note: Completes military reconnaissance of the field, then adds a falconry use. The abbreviated Itẽ starts with capital I, and cõ- is printed with a terminal mark.

runs.text: falcão os que eſpreitão, & notão onde pouſa al-

lines.note: In falconry, these are the watchers who observe where a bird settles. The final al- continues into the abbreviated alguma on the next row.
Completes alguma ave; toomi wo oku means posting lookouts. The Portuguese vi continues into vigias without a clearly printed line-end hyphen.
Completes vigias and equates them with scouts or spies. This short row closes the example of posting lookouts.

Toonoke is the transitive verb for putting something far away. Only a tiny triangular remnant survives above the second o: the supplied caron in Touonǒqe is retained provisionally, without treating it as a secure long-vowel reading or erasing the visible mark.
Completes the transitive definition as separating the object to a distant place. The enclitic object in apartarla is preserved as printed.
Toonoki supplies the corresponding intransitive forms, to move away or become distant. The two Portuguese reflexives contrast with the object-taking definition immediately above.
Toori here means tenor, nature, or kind. Tsukai no toori begins the example about the substance of a message, divided after to-.

runs.text: Dizer a ſuſtancia, ou teor do reca-

lines.note: Tsukai no toori wo yuu means stating the substance or tenor of the message. The caron on yǔ is visible; reca- continues into recado.
Sonata no toori no bun introduces a comparison with the addressee or the addressee's stated account. The Portuguese da mesma continues its explanation below.

runs.text: maneira, ou teor q̃ vos. Itẽ, O teor do q̃ dizeis.

lines.note: Completes the alternatives: in the same manner or tenor as you, or the tenor of what you say. Both abbreviated q̃ forms and Itẽ retain their printed tildes.
Toori gives the verb to pass or go through. Michi wo begins the example about travelling along a road.

Michi wo tooru means passing along the road; incidental dark ink crosses the verb without removing its reading. The following Qiǒuo is the object for a scripture or book in the next example: enlargement supports dotted i, not OCR u, and a caron over o.
Ichibu mitooru describes going through a whole volume. The Portuguese confirms reading or passing through a book from beginning to end; prin- begins principio.
Completes from beginning to end, preserving the printed ocabo. Kookai kokoro ni tooru then introduces repentance penetrating or reaching the heart.
Completes the Japanese tooru and renders the phrase as heartfelt contrition. The spiritual sense is an extension of passage or penetration.
Toori is now the noun passage or passing. Michi no begins an expression for the route or course of a road.
Michi no toori is explained by michi no suji, the course of a road. The printed ſugi spelling is retained; fi- begins fieira in the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: eira do caminho. ¶ Item, Hũa bebida, ou

lines.note: Completes the road's course or line, then gives a drinking-related sense. The following rows explain the social act rather than a variety of beverage.

runs.text: beberete que fazem muitos juntos bebendo cada

lines.note: The drinking is done together by many people, each taking a turn. Cada introduces the distributive phrase completed by hum below.

runs.text: hum, & afaſtando ſe como quando o ſenhor dà

lines.note: Each person drinks and then moves away. The comparison introduces a lord giving the drinking cup to his servants.

runs.text: o Sacazzuqui aos criados. Mas cõmummente

lines.note: The Japanese cup-name Sacazzuqui is embedded in the Portuguese description of the lord serving his retainers. Its type remains italic in this impression; the sentence then introduces the more usual name.
Votouori is the more commonly used designation for this shared drinking round. It is an upright Japanese term inside the Portuguese explanation, not a separate headword.
Tooriawase means encountering something while passing. The supplied ſuru principal form is retained even though it differs from a simple modern stem expansion.

runs.text: trarſe com algũa couſa, ou acertar de ver al-

lines.note: Continues encountering something or happening to see something. Both alternatives depend on the passing-by context, and al- continues into alguma below.
Completes the chance-encounter definition: seeing something while going past. The abbreviated gũa is the continuation of al- from the preceding row.
Toosaburai is a designated place or building for certain retainers. The final on- begins onde, locating the activity described next.

runs.text: de cuſtumão eſtar os criados honrados dalgum

lines.note: Specifies that a lord's honored retainers customarily stay there. The historical cuſtumão and the contraction dalgum are preserved.
Completes the possessive phrase of some lord. This genuine short body line closes the definition of the retainers' room.

Tooshi is the transitive verb to pass something through, allow it through, or cause it to pass. The l of algũa is largely lost: its upper remnant survives between a and gũa, supporting this chosen restoration of the damaged word.
Completes the causative gloss, then illustrates opening the middle to let someone pass. The Japanese toosu is divided after touo-.

runs.text: Dar caminho a alguem pollo meyo.

lines.note: Completes toosu and translates the example as giving someone a path through the middle. The scan has pollo with two l letters, correcting the draft's polo.
Ikidoori wo toosu means maintaining resentment or allowing it to persist. The Portuguese durar o rancor identifies the figurative sustained-emotion sense.
Nozomi wo toosu means carrying one's desire or intention through. The Portuguese begins proceeding onward with the desire.
Completes pursuing the desire until fulfilling it. The next example begins mune wo toosu, with the printed terminal hyphen retained before yoona.

Mune wo toosu yoona itami describes pain that seems to pass through the chest. The visible singular parece and single long s in atraueſar are preserved despite modern grammatical or spelling expectations.
Completes the penetrating-pain example as pain through the chest or heart. It closes the final illustration of toosu.
Toozakari is to move away or become distant. The principal forms and both Portuguese reflexives point to an intransitive sense.

runs.text: Hũa laya de verruma de Iapão.

lines.note: Tooshigiri is a kind of Japanese boring tool or auger. The entry supplies no more precise construction details, so the note does not assign a modern tool subtype.

runs.text: Frecha delgada pera voar, ou che-

lines.note: Tooya is a slender arrow intended to fly or reach far. The final che- starts chegar; its initial c and tall h replace the OCR reading abe-.
Completes chegar longe, reaching a great distance. It belongs to the arrow's purpose, not a separate lexical entry.
Tooyama denotes a distant mountain. The Portuguese adjective on the next line restates longe.
Completes the mountain definition as distant. The visible long-s/t group restores diſtante from OCR ditante; the short continuation is the final body row, above the separate signature and catchword.
